timeline.author: Tom Denley

timeline.body:
Motivation:

A BoundedInputStream was recently introduced to protect against attacks where a large file was placed on the server.  Unfortunately, this has an issue preventing it from reading the last bytes of a file where the buffer size would take the total bytes over the set bound, when reading just the remaining bytes in the file fits underneath the set bound.

Modification:

Adjusted the behaviour of BoundedInputStream to, where appropriate, read 1 more byte than the set bound, to see if the file terminates at this point, in which case there is no need to throw the exception

Result:

Fixes #14479.
The original motivation for checking for `num` was to fail before starting the actual read (no need to try reading if we know we are going out of bound). Is it possible to preserve that behavior?

reply.body: `maxBytesRead` already protects from "don't read more than allowed", but it is worth reading if the requested `len` is larger than we can based on remaining from `maxBytesRead`?

> The original motivation for checking for `num` was to fail before starting the actual read (no need to try reading if we know we are going out of bound). Is it possible to preserve that behavior?

No, it is not possible to do that.  You have no idea when the underlying stream will terminate, so just because the request is to read `len` bytes, you cannot assume that many bytes will actually be read.

Ok, so for the cases when the caller doesn't know about the underlying file size and the `BoundedInputStream` protection, it can still request more which doesn't mean we read that much. Makes sense to me, thanks for clarifying.

timeline.body:
> checking the bytes consumed after the fact is also doesn't seem right.

It is impossible to do this correctly without attempting to read from the underlying stream.  There is simply no way of telling how many bytes will actually be read without attempting to read them.

At the moment, we have a version of netty out in the wild that is logging stacktraces every time it is started.

> We could split the difference and let the bulk-read operation read up to the limit, and only throw if reads are done at the limit and beyond.

The code that I submitted is already doing this.  It only reads up to the limit, and throws if the underlying stream is not consumed at this point.
What's the idea with potentially throwing after we've done the read?

reply.body: Because we can't know if we hit the bound until after we have done the read
